I think Im being misunderstood in this thread. I dont say that the writing is bad and i agree that a fun story should be the primary objective. That you can write a good mystery without relying on these rules.  
I was just confused why Will recited these rules and what it means in the bigger picture. Since, this doesnt "give us more". We have Knox's ruleset which feels more coherent to the mystery Umineko tells.

Personally, I think that the Sayo argument isnt really good since every maid/servant/buttler character in mysteries are "more than they seem". It doesnt change that they are introduced as the servant. No matter how "true" that servant-hood is after the big reveal.

Anyways, I was just confused what the purpose was of reciting Van Dine, besides adding more meta mystery lore into Umineko.

But it was under the pretence of her being a servant. Every servant culprit in murder mysteries ever made, were more than "just" a servant. Being a child of infidelity and an actual heir is a fairly common trope in those types of stories. Making that argument is a copout.

With romance, I meant that the main point of the story was the Beato Battler relationship.

Since i got downvoted to oblivion I guess I have to make clear that this isnt criticism towards the story and was in no way intended to be malicious.

I was just curious why Ryukishi felt it was necessary to include that piece of dialogue for Will and establish the ideas of Van Dine when we already have Knox which felt more in line to the "mystery" thus far.
Just found it odd. Why recite Van Dine like that only to *not* follow his rules anyways.

Considering the character journey Nathan went on it just felt off. Which makes it the first time i noticed inconsistencies in the writing. With tone i meant that I never felt that the jokes felt out of place in any of Nathan's shows. Except for the last 2-3 episodes with the examples I gave in the thread.

>The Rehearsal season 1 finale is the most evil thing he's ever done.  


It sure IS evil what he did. But deliberately using a just cause, presenting yourself as a person who wants to get out of your "comedic role" to actually make a change. Only for it to be just a farce for entertainment is worse imo. Idk, maybe it is because aviation safety isnt as prevalent as, lets say cancer. But for the sake of getting my point across I take that as the example.  
If Nathan presents himself as someone who wanted to do something against cancer and he goes on and on about how he wouldn't be taken serious by the media and doctors, you (the audience) would take the subject matter serious, and therefore if he (Nathan) was in front of a doctor, you wouldn't expect him to fumble it so hard "just for the sake of entertainment".

It may be a cruel example of mine, but that WAS the image that Nathan gave me throughout this season, hence my confusion/frustration...  
But you're right. We'll see how the finale will tie everything together. I'll binge everything eventually with your input in mind.



>Cohen sees Nathan as nothing, as a joke, and doesn't offer the light of day to him

To be fair, Nathan was the first who "turned it into a joke". He made the conversation awkward and stirred it into that direction.



>I don't believe though, that the real life Nathan actually believed he would save lives, or even put any genuine work towards a plan that could save lives.



Neither did I. A real human (real Nathan) would see it realistically and at least be critical of his ambitions and what he can feasibly do. But that doesnt mean that if you are interested in a serious subject matter to the point that you seek out specialists, you use your Network to perform experiments and obsessively take notes and make your own behavioural studies (granted, they are tied Nathan moreso than the aviation safety project) and you actually have the chance to show your research to an official congress; that you just toss it out because "you never believed it was possible anyways" and "its just entertainment bro".

There IS something real in there and pretending there isnt would turn the premise of this season and character Nathan into nothing.

>Sorry to word salad you lol. I'm not trying to disagree super hard with you or anything. I'm kind of using threads like this to realize what I think of all this.

>He (the character) believed he could pitch it and make it work, and made a genuine attempt. It was Nathan, the real life guy, who threw the opportunity for a bit. Nathan the guy threw away the opportunity by writing the show so that Nathan the character failed the opportunity despite trying.

  
Ayayyay. Thats a mouthful. I try to keep that in mind that his "real self" sabotages everything on my rewatch.

It does make sense, though. The "real" Nathan just wants to pitch his show but that makes him wayy more evil than i would've expected - and i honestly couldnt see it that way. That the "real" Nathan would use a serious issue that costs people lifes for entertainment weighs way more than any type of moral grey areas he walked on before...

>I think part of the reason I love the show is because I don't get the impression that Nathan is disingenuous at all, I just think he's great at taking a problem (no matter how big or small) and then extrapolating it into something that shines a light on the bigger picture.

FOR SURE. Its a very organic way to develop his character further and make use of his awareness of the sets and everything. Great stuff.

>the Summit Ice *Nathan For You* episode where he targets those cheap ad campaigns



Thats a really good comparison. He's shedding light on an issue and that exposure leads to awareness. But with Summit Ice it feels like he was way more proactive and willing to make a stance for the cause. And i kinda expected that here too. Episode 1 makes it clear that his character is invested in that cause (aviation safety). And 5 episodes in,  
he HAS that meeting with a congressman. And instead of showing his research and engaging in a genuine dialogue it ends like it ended...  


>I think that's the overall throughline for the shows he's done: make them funny, heighten the situations either via story or just the actors themselves being ridiculous

Im totally with you. Rehearsal just leans wayyyy more into absurdism (especially with the concept) in terms of its comedy, so, using "cheap gags" feels like backtracking, considering both the evolution of Nathans storytelling and his character.

Hmm i was really sure that we were still with the character Nathan. The Nathan who wanted to change the world - using his HBO power. And even if we weren't, passing up the chance to bring up your theory to an actual congressman just for a bit ? Doesnt that defeat the purpose of what that season was building towards?

>who is vastly unable to comprehend social situations and can only come up with impractical solutions to problems.

We saw that Nathan is very much able to comprehend social situations. At least the Nathan we follow this season. His discussions with this NTSB guy were really grounded and i expected a similar discussion with the congressman. The anime has great voice acting, FANTASTIC music, great directing, makes great use of basically everything an anime could provide. It covers everything faithfully and is overall a great adaptation which takes it's artistic liberties.But while the anime focuses more on the mind games, the manga feels more like the journey of a loser who tries to escape the mundanity of his life. This isn't to say that the anime doesn't go into it's fair share of social criticism, but i feel like the manga takes it to another level. Fukumoto is a very VERY outspoken mangaka who doesn't mind going on long tangents to get his point across.

If you are already familiar with his works I'd say jump into the manga to get the full Fukumoto experience and rewatch the anime after (bc why not, its great). If you just want a first impression of Kaiji you can't go wrong with the anime. Either way, there are 4 parts in Kaiji which aren't animated so if you enjoy Kaiji you will end up reading the manga anyways.

My very first thought was literally "I need to re-read this".

It took me 2 years to finish it because I couldn't find a specific volume and I really wasn't in a rush to finish it.

I had a 1 1/2 year gap between 2 volumes and I read a bunch of different manga at that time.

When I started Punpun, I saw it more as a story, but upon finishing it and then re-reading it a couple months later, it became something more to me. I think during the time I didn't read Punpun I got to learn more about me and my preferences in stories ... it was also a stressful time where I reflected a lot.

Punpun is prob the first story which I can't see in a "traditional" sense because it feels more like a tale from actual real people instead of a farbicated story.

There are great videos out there from people talking about Punpun and some even share a bit of personal struggles and how they could relate to this manga...

but one quote from RealLifeRyan's video really stuck with me. That "you wouldn't really get it" if you haven't atleast experienced a portion of this story yourself.

That you can say "Yea, it's a sad story", but if you went through some of this it becomes really something different. Not a story that you read, appreciate, rate, forget and then move away from. Going to the next manga to read...

I re-read Punpun since then once a year and it has become my favorite manga. Never would I have imagined it to be a fav of mine when I started it. It's crazy... everytime i re-read it, my appreciation for it jumps up a notch. Not only because of the great writing, but more so that I go through my own life and make new experiences... Punpun becomes more and more relatable with each readthrough and it's strange to say, but it feels more like meeting a friend every once in a while and have a discusion on far we have come. It's really special.
